quirks: All vital records are organized at the parish (prestegjeld) level — identify the parish before browsing the 18,000+ digitized volumes; use the indexed marriage collection (1468080) to find the entry and thereby identify the parish.
Patronymic naming: men took -sen (son of father's first name), women took -datter; surnames changed each generation. Search on first name + approximate year when surname variants yield no results.

Church records (kirkebøker) are the primary marriage source for the entire pre-civil registration period (~pre-1890s). Civil marriage indexes on Digitalarkivet.no begin c.1863 and broaden in the 1880s-1890s.
Norway, Marriages 1660-1926 (collection 1468080) has 1.3 million indexed records but ZERO images — retrieve images from Norway, Church Books 1797-1958 (collection 4237104) or Digitalarkivet.no.

Most parish-level kirkebok volumes on FamilySearch are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. Identifying the parish from an indexed collection entry is the prerequisite to image-browsing.

Digitalarkivet.no (https://digitalarkivet.no/) is the Norwegian national digital archive and should be searched in parallel with FamilySearch — it holds civil marriage records, emigration records, and additional church record scans.
Records are in Norwegian / Dano-Norwegian; marriage entries use standard formulaic terminology. Key fields: dato (date), navn (name), foreldre (parents).

# Locality Guide: Norway (1820–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Country:** Norway (standardPlace: `Norway`)
- **State church:** Church of Norway (Lutheran) — kept primary vital records
- **Naming custom:** Patronymic: men `-sen`, women `-datter` from father's first name; changed each generation; fixed surnames not standard until 1923 Act.

## Available record types

### Church records (kirkebøker) — PRIMARY SOURCE
- Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926 (FS col. 1468080): 1,330,979 indexed records; **0 images** — index only
- Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958 (FS col. 4237104): 14,398,439 records; 1,288,153 images — indexed + images
- Norway, Baptisms, 1634–1927 (FS col. 1467014): 5,277,294 records
- 18,963+ digitized volumes (marriage/religious types) in FamilySearch image archive; most are **0% indexed, browse-only**, in Norwegian
- Also on Digitalarkivet.no (free): https://digitalarkivet.no/

### Civil registration
- Civil Marriage Index 1863–1919 and related sets on Digitalarkivet.no; broader coverage from 1880s–1893 depending on parish.

### Censuses (FamilySearch)
- 1865 (col. 3756102), 1870 (col. 4135961), 1875 (col. 1529106), 1891 (col. 4067726), 1900 (col. 3744863)

### Probate
- Norway, Probate Index Cards, 1640–1903 (col. 1661306): 1,058,029 records

### Migration
- Norway, Emigration Records, 1874–1960 on Ancestry (col. 61757)

## Research tips
- Identify the parish first using the indexed marriage collection, then retrieve images.
- Search censuses (1865, 1875) to place the subject in a specific parish.
- Search Digitalarkivet.no in parallel with FamilySearch.
- Records in Norwegian/Dano-Norwegian; key terms: dato, navn, foreldre.

entry.rationale: FamilySearch collection 1468080, 'Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926', contains 1,330,979 indexed records (personCount confirmed by collections_search). This is the highest-probability first item: search by groom name 'Anders Monsen' and bride name 'Unna Halsteinsdatter'. Norwegian marriage registers (kirkebøker) typically recorded date, parish, groom and bride, both fathers' names (confirming the patronymics), witnesses, and ages. Per loc_001: collection 1468080 has 0 images — once a match is found, retrieve the original image from collection 4237104 or Digitalarkivet.no. Try variant spellings: Mohnsen, Andersen (in case of early fixed-name use), Halsteindatter, Halsteins Datter.

FamilySearch collection 4237104, 'Norway, Church Books, 1797-1958', contains 14,398,439 indexed records and 1,288,153 images (collections_search). Broader than collection 1468080: includes baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations in one searchable corpus with original images. If the marriage entry does not surface in pli_001, search this collection directly by name. Also use this collection to retrieve the original kirkebok image after pli_001 identifies the entry (since 1468080 has no images). Searching here may also surface a baptism or confirmation for Anders Monsen that names his father Mons Monsen and anchors the family to a specific parish.

FAN item. FamilySearch holds indexed Norwegian censuses for 1865 (col. 3756102, 1,688,075 records with images), 1875 (col. 1529106, 333,541 records), and 1891 (col. 4067726, 2,727,197 records with images). Search each for Anders Monsen. A census hit will: (a) identify the specific parish (prestegjeld) where the family lived — the prerequisite for browsing unindexed kirkebok volumes (per loc_001 quirk: all records organized at parish level); (b) confirm Unna Halsteinsdatter or Unna Monsen as co-resident spouse, establishing the marriage occurred before the census year; (c) show children's ages, bracketing the approximate marriage year. As a FAN item: the household enumeration names neighbors and household members who shared the same church community, providing context for where the marriage record was filed and potentially naming relatives of both Anders and Unna.

Digitalarkivet.no (https://digitalarkivet.no/) is the Norwegian National Archives' digital repository and the authoritative source for Norwegian historical records. It holds church records (kirkebøker), civil marriage indexes (from c.1863 per external_links_search data showing sets covering 1863-1919, 1883-1919, 1887-1910, 1891-1908, 1892-1912, 1893+), emigration records, and indexes not fully mirrored on FamilySearch. Since the marriage date is unknown, search both church-era (pre-1890s) and civil-era registers. Execute via search-external-sites skill. The site is free.

Full-text co-occurrence search fallback. Per loc_001: 18,963 digitized volumes for Norway marriage/religious records exist, most at 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable (browse-only). If the indexed collections (pli_001, pli_002) fail to surface the marriage — because the specific parish's volumes are not name-indexed — run a full-text search using 'Monsen' and 'Halstein' (Unna's father's name, embedded in her patronymic 'Halsteinsdatter') as a co-occurrence across the Norwegian church book corpus via the search-full-text skill. This tactic targets AI-transcribed page text from volumes that are not name-indexed. Do not scope to a specific collection id; run unscoped across the full corpus. Also try 'Anders' + 'Unna' as a name-pair co-occurrence if the surname search yields nothing.

The 1891 census for Voss specifically (imageGroupNumber 107236654, 7,667 images, 100% searchable) is within this collection. The 1891 census records the household head, spouse, children, and their birthplaces and ages. A hit for Anders Monsen in Voss/Hordaland would: (a) confirm Unna Halsteinsdatter/Monsen as his wife, establishing that the marriage occurred before 1891; (b) give the specific parish (prestegjeld or sokn) where the family lived — the key for then locating the unindexed kirkebok marriage volume on Digitalarkivet.no; (c) show children's birth years, bracketing when the marriage took place. # Locality Guide: Norway (1820–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Country:** Norway (Kingdom of Norway; standardPlace: `"Norway"`, FamilySearch place ID 40)
- **Administrative center:** Christiania (Oslo) — seat of national government
- **State church:** Church of Norway (Lutheran), which kept the primary vital records throughout this period
- **Population during period:** Population data unavailable (Pop Stats API unreachable)
- **Religious denominations:** Overwhelmingly Lutheran (Church of Norway); small communities of other Protestants after the Dissenters Act of 1845; Roman Catholics were a tiny minority
- **Naming custom:** Patronymic surnames in the 19th century — men took `-sen` (son of father's first name), women took `-datter` (daughter of father's first name); these changed with each generation. Fixed hereditary surnames did not become standard until the Surnames Act of 1923.

## Boundary changes
- Norway was governed as a dual monarchy with Sweden, 1814–1905 (union dissolved 1905). Records were created by Norwegian civil and church authorities throughout; Swedish records are not relevant to Norwegian vital events.
- The target parish for Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter is unknown. The specific parish must be identified — all vital records are organized at the parish (prestegjeld) level, not at the national or county level.

## Available record types

### Church records (kirkebøker) — PRIMARY SOURCE
- **Pre-civil registration:** The Church of Norway kept marriage, baptism, burial, and confirmation registers from the 17th century onward. These are the definitive source for marriages before civil registration.
- **Record type:** Marriage entries (*copulerte*) recorded groom's name, bride's name, date, parish, and typically both fathers' names (patronymic). Witnesses and banns are often included.
- **Language:** Norwegian (Bokmål/Dano-Norwegian), with older entries in Danish
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - **Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926** (collection [1468080](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1468080)): 1,330,979 indexed records; 3,519,558 persons — **no images** (index only; images must be accessed separately)
  - **Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958** (collection [4237104](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/4237104)): 14,398,439 indexed records; 1,288,153 images — **indexed + images**
  - **Norway, Baptisms, 1634–1927** (collection [1467014](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1467014)): 5,277,294 records
  - **Norway, Burials, 1666–1927** (collection [1468081](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1468081)): 719,685 records
- **Digitized parish-level volumes:** 18,963 digitized volumes matching religious/marriage records for Norway 1820–1900 exist in FamilySearch's image archive; however, the vast majority of parish-level volumes are **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — they must be browsed image-by-image. The parish (prestegjeld) of the marriage must be identified first before browsing is practical.
- **Also on:** [Digitalarkivet.no](https://digitalarkivet.no/) (The Digital Archive, National Archives of Norway) — the definitive Norwegian national repository, with church records and indexes free to search. Link: https://digitalarkivet.no/

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Civil marriage registration:** Based on external link data from FS-curated resources, civil marriage records appear in Digitalarkivet.no from approximately 1863 onward (Civil Marriage Index, 1863–1919), with broader coverage from the 1880s–1893 period depending on municipality. Multiple distinct civil marriage record sets from Digitalarkivet.no cover 1883–1919, 1887–1910, 1891–1908, 1892–1912, 1893+, 1894–1901, 1894–1904, 1895–1907, 1895–1911, 1896+, 1900.
- **Implication for this research:** If the marriage occurred before civil registration became widespread in the relevant parish (roughly pre-1890s), the church register (kirkebok) will be the only contemporaneous record.
- **FamilySearch wiki pages:** Unavailable (wiki-query-api offline); the FamilySearch Wiki article on Norway Vital Records could not be retrieved.

- **Digitized probate records:** Scanned probate records available at [media.digitalarkivet.no](https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/sk/browse).

### Migration / emigration records
- Large-scale emigration to North America, especially 1865–1920, is well documented.
- **Ancestry:** Norway, Emigration Records, 1874–1960 (collection 61757)

### Online repositories

| [Digitalarkivet.no](https://digitalarkivet.no) | Church records (kirkebøker); Civil marriage records 1863–1919+; Emigration; Probate scans | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 18,963 digitized volumes matching religious/marriage records for Norway 1820–1900; the first page of 50 was examined. The next page token is present; the remaining ~18,900+ volumes were not individually reviewed. The two main indexed collections (1468080, 4237104) cover the relevant period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Riksarkivet (National Archives of Norway) | Original church registers, probate, court records | In-person / scans on Digitalarkivet.no |
| Local statsarkiv (regional archives, 8 branches) | Regional copies of church registers, local court records | In-person or through Digitalarkivet.no |
| Local parishes | Some original registers may remain with the parish | By appointment |

## Records NOT online
- Not all parish-level kirkebok volumes are fully indexed; many are images-only, accessible only by browsing after identifying the parish.
- Pre-1865 census records (e.g., 1801 census) are separately held; the 1801 census is searchable at [digitalarkivet.no/en/census/search/1801](https://www.digitalarkivet.no/en/census/search/1801).

## Known record losses
- No major nationwide destruction. Some local parish records have gaps; completeness must be verified per parish.

## Research tips
- **Identify the parish first.** Every church record in Norway is organized at the prestegjeld (parish) level. Without a parish name, browsing is impractical across 18,000+ volumes. Use the indexed collections (Norway, Marriages 1660–1926; Norway, Church Books 1797–1958) to find the marriage entry and thereby identify the parish.
- **The patronymic naming system means names shift each generation.** Anders Monsen's father was named Mons; his children would take "Anderssen/Andersdatter." Anna Andersdatter in the tree may be their child. This aids generation-linking but makes index searching harder — search on first name + approximate year if surname variants fail.
- **Start with the indexed marriage collection on FamilySearch** (collection 1468080 — Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926), then retrieve the image from the Church Books collection (4237104) or Digitalarkivet.no for the full record content.
- **Censuses confirm household and parish.** The 1865 and 1875 censuses (indexed on FamilySearch) can place Anders Monsen in a specific parish, unlocking the relevant kirkebok volume.
- **Digitalarkivet.no** is the authoritative Norwegian digital archive and should be searched in parallel with FamilySearch — it holds records not mirrored on FamilySearch and has its own marriage indexes.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for Norway** could not be retrieved (server offline at time of survey). Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway when available for additional research guidance.
- **Records are in Norwegian / Dano-Norwegian.** Marriage entries use standard formulaic Latin/Norwegian terminology; key fields are: dato (date), navn (name), foreldre (parents).
